intro: A pilgrims’ hymn frames the restless music of Venus’s mountain. This concert-band arrangement transfers Wagner’s opposition between sustained chorale and rushing figuration to wind, brass and percussion.
question: What changes when the opening hymn returns after the fast music?

relations.label: The Venus song returns higher
relations.basis: The broad song in the fast Venusberg section is restated in the renewed fast span. The five-semitone upward pitch-class shift is consistent with its move to another tonal level; the listening notes distinguish this song from the pilgrims’ hymn. CENS diagonal mean 0.940, sustained 34.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift +5 semitones and time offset 174 s (cache/form/wagner-tannhauser-overture.txt, candidate 1; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

relations.label: The pilgrims’ hymn returns
relations.basis: The overture’s closing frame restores the pilgrims’ hymn after the Venusberg music. The earlier excerpt comes from the hymn’s first broad statement, while the later one follows the return marked near 665 s. CENS diagonal mean 0.934, sustained 14 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 527 s (cache/form/wagner-tannhauser-overture.txt, candidate 5; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: The pilgrims before Venus
cues.text: A slow hymn opens the overture. In the opera it belongs to pilgrims travelling to Rome; its sustained phrases establish a contrast with the restless writing associated with Venus’s mountain.
cues.evidence: Marc Mandel’s Boston Symphony account identifies the opening pilgrims’ music. The recording’s quiet, low-activity first minute supports the opening span, without a note-level alignment.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A long melodic line
cues.text: Follow the hymn across the smaller divisions of its phrases. In a band performance, the continuity of a long line depends on breath and balance rather than on a section of bowed strings.
cues.evidence: This is a listening point about sustained writing in the documented band arrangement. No particular player’s breath or instrumental handover has been identified.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Harmony within a slow phrase
cues.text: Listen for changing harmony beneath the sustained manner of the opening. A slowly moving melody can contain tension before any quicker surface motion begins.
cues.evidence: The report shows changes in pitch balance around 1:10–1:30 while attack density remains low. It does not supply a reliable chord-by-chord analysis of the band transcription.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A court post in Dresden
cues.text: Wagner became conductor of the Royal Saxon Court in Dresden in February 1843. He composed Tannhäuser while holding that post and conducted its first performance there on 19 October 1845.
cues.evidence: Mandel documents the appointment, composition chronology and premiere: https://www.bso.org/works/overture-and-venusberg-music-from-tannh%C3%A4user
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: The first broad expansion
cues.text: The opening music grows into its first forceful statement. Listen for the sustained line against quicker accompanying movement: different rates of motion can occupy the same texture.
cues.evidence: The score combines hymn and moving accompaniment. Relative level and detected attacks increase around 2:20–2:30; the analysis does not establish which band instruments carry each part.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Long notes, moving accompaniment
cues.text: Follow the slower melody without losing the quicker figures around it. Accompanying motion can keep a sustained phrase active without making the main tune more elaborate.
cues.evidence: This is a score-based comparison across the first full hymn span. The report shows sustained higher level and continuing attacks around 2:55–3:15.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Receding from the first crest
cues.text: The opening’s forceful statement is followed by a substantial retreat. Listen across the falling intensity as the slow span prepares to give way to the contrasting centre.
cues.evidence: Relative level falls around 3:15–3:20 and continues down through 3:50. The cue concerns the broad withdrawal, not an exact instrumental exit.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: A pilgrimage with consequences
cues.text: After leaving Venus’s realm, Tannhäuser praises her during a song contest at the Wartburg. Elisabeth protects him from the other singers’ anger, and he joins pilgrims seeking absolution in Rome. The overture’s contrasting themes draw on this dramatic conflict.
cues.evidence: The plot and the overture’s use of music from the opera are set out by Mandel: https://www.bso.org/works/overture-and-venusberg-music-from-tannh%C3%A4user
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: The Venusberg span
cues.text: In the fast centre, shorter figures replace the hymn’s sustained manner. Compare the restless movement with the opening’s broad phrases rather than expecting a completely separate piece.
cues.evidence: Mandel identifies the Venusberg music after the opening pilgrims’ span. Renewed activity around 5:00–5:15 suggests its placement here; the transition is not precisely aligned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Figures rather than a hymn
cues.text: Attend to the short figures as well as any continuous melody. Their repeated movement helps maintain the centre’s contrasting character even through quieter phrases.
cues.evidence: The score’s faster centre supplies the listening point. The report shows continuing attacks around 5:35–5:50 at relatively low level, without identifying individual parts.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A song within the fast centre
cues.text: The central music includes Tannhäuser’s hymn in praise of Venus. A broader tune appears within the restless setting: the same character who seeks absolution also gives this opposing world a lyrical voice.
cues.evidence: Mandel identifies the hymn to Venus in this position. The more sustained span around 6:00–6:15 and following swell suggest its location in the transcription; its first note is not timed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Another forceful crest
cues.text: The central span builds towards a large crest of its own. Compare its weight with the earlier pilgrims’ music, while keeping their different kinds of melodic movement in mind.
cues.evidence: Relative level remains high around 6:40–7:05 and rises further near 7:10–7:15. The comparison is within this recording, not between performances.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: A quieter inner episode
cues.text: The forceful centre gives way to a quieter episode before its next large expansion. Listen for smaller gestures within the reduced scale rather than expecting the opening hymn to return immediately.
cues.evidence: Mandel describes a contrasting central episode. A strong change around 7:38 and lower relative level through about 8:10 support this approximate placement; the original orchestral scoring is not assigned to the band.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Sustained writing gathers weight
cues.text: The surrounding passage shifts towards longer-held sound before another increase in force. Compare the phrase’s changing activity with its changing volume: these need not move together.
cues.evidence: Detected attacks become sparse around 8:50–9:05 before relative level rises through 9:15. The detector cannot establish every articulation or identify an instrumental group.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: The Paris revision
cues.text: For Paris in 1861, Wagner expanded the Venusberg scene and supplied a first-act ballet. The production faced organised disruption and was withdrawn after three performances. Joining the overture directly to the expanded Bacchanale was a later change, not the original Paris arrangement.
cues.evidence: Mandel distinguishes the 1861 production from the later conflated Overture and Bacchanale: https://www.bso.org/works/overture-and-venusberg-music-from-tannh%C3%A4user
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Colour and weight can diverge
cues.text: Across the later fast span, compare changes of tone colour with changes of force. A passage need not become quieter and darker at the same rate.
cues.evidence: The report’s spectral balance shifts towards higher frequencies around 10:10–10:25 while relative level recedes after 10:15. This does not establish a particular register or instrument.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: Room for the returning hymn
cues.text: The late fast span releases its pressure before the broader opening manner returns. Listen across the retreat rather than expecting the ending to begin with an immediate full-volume statement.
cues.evidence: The report shows a sharp fall in relative level and attack density around 11:00–11:10. The score supplies the subsequent return; its exact entrance is not inferred from the fall alone.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: The opening music returns
cues.text: The pilgrims’ music returns below the eventual closing intensity. Compare its long phrases with the opening: the conclusion develops music already heard rather than introducing a new triumphant theme.
cues.evidence: The score’s self-contained overture reprises the pilgrims’ music. The sustained span around 11:10–12:00 resembles the opening profile and supports this approximate placement.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A work never settled
cues.text: Wagner revised Tannhäuser repeatedly. In her diary for 23 January 1883, Cosima recorded his remark that he still owed the world Tannhäuser. The statement comes from her account of their conversation, written shortly before his death.
cues.evidence: Mandel quotes Cosima’s dated diary entry and traces the revisions: https://www.bso.org/works/overture-and-venusberg-music-from-tannh%C3%A4user
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: The hymn gains weight
cues.text: The returning hymn expands towards the conclusion while quicker movement continues around it. Keep the slower phrase and the accompanying figures separate as the texture grows fuller.
cues.evidence: The score combines the final chorale with moving accompaniment. Relative level rises around 12:35–12:45 and remains high; the precise allocation among band instruments is not established.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Keep hearing the inner movement
cues.text: Do not follow only the strongest melody. Listen for continuing movement around the hymn’s longer notes: the conclusion brings contrasting rates of motion into the same texture.
cues.evidence: This is a score-based listening point for the final hymn span, not a claim of an instrumental handover at 13:20.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The closing expansion
cues.text: The last span sustains greater recorded weight than the hymn’s first full statement. Compare the proportions of the two expansions, not just the fact that a familiar melody has returned.
cues.evidence: The closing span around 13:55–14:10 has higher relative level than most of the first broad statement around 2:25–3:15. No claim is made about absolute concert-hall loudness.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: A self-contained ending
cues.text: The closing hymn and its final decay complete the overture. This arrangement does not continue directly into the expanded Venusberg ballet, as the later combined Overture and Bacchanale does.
cues.evidence: The score versions are distinguished in Mandel’s account. The return of the opening profile followed by decay around 14:15–14:20 supports a self-contained ending; the last attack is not precisely timed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The hymn gains a moving upper layer
transitions.how: The hymn expands within B♭ major rather than changing into a new theme. In Sousa’s band score, the brass reinforce its long notes while the first clarinets acquire the running upper figures that an orchestra gives to strings. The bass keeps the harmonic steps clear beneath these different rates of movement. The join is additive: a line previously carried by a smaller wind group becomes a public statement, with a new, faster surface around it but no change from the opening’s three-beat metre.
transitions.evidence: First broad climax is mapped at 145 s, during the analysis rise at 2:20–2:30. Sousa’s score, opening build and first full hymn, establishes the concert B♭ setting and clarinet figuration. Unlike the earlier cues, these concert-pitch statements use the band score linked beside this Director’s Choice recording: https://www.marineband.marines.mil/Audio-Resources/Sheet-Music/ ; https://www.marineband.marines.mil/Portals/175/Docs/Sheet%20Music/Tannhauser/tannhauser_score.pdf?ver=2018-10-17-112418-240 .

transitions.title: Quiet wind motion replaces the hymn
transitions.how: The opening hymn has receded into quiet wind chords before the Allegro changes 3/4 to common time. Sousa gives the first running entry to the lower clarinet parts; the heavier bass and brass foundation falls away while upper winds answer with short, chromatically inflected figures. Wagner does not use a loud cutoff to announce Venus’s realm. Small moving cells emerge from the depleted end of the B♭-major hymn, and their changing harmonies replace the chorale’s more readily followed cadential steps.
transitions.evidence: Venusberg is mapped at 310 s. The report has very low level at 4:45–4:55 and renewed attacks around 5:10. Sousa’s score, printed pp. 19–20, shows the Allegro, metre change and quiet clarinet-led entry; this is an approximate span rather than a timestamp for bar 82: https://www.marineband.marines.mil/Portals/175/Docs/Sheet%20Music/Tannhauser/tannhauser_score.pdf?ver=2018-10-17-112418-240 .

transitions.title: The full band leaves a solo thread
transitions.how: After the forceful central crest, the band sheds its heavy accompaniment and the phrase briefly holds back. In the quieter Venusberg episode, Sousa places the sustained solo line in clarinet against little moving figures in the upper woodwinds; the orchestral original’s divided violin texture is not what is sounding here. The bass largely withdraws, so the melody and chromatic inner parts carry the harmonic continuity. The join reduces weight without eliminating motion: the quick figures become a soft background instead of the main event.
transitions.evidence: Quieter central episode is mapped at 458 s, the report’s strongest boundary at 7:38, followed by lower level through 8:10. Sousa’s score, printed pp. 39–42, shows the retreat, Un poco ritenuto and clarinet-led episode at rehearsal D. Exact bar-to-time alignment is not claimed: https://www.marineband.marines.mil/Portals/175/Docs/Sheet%20Music/Tannhauser/tannhauser_score.pdf?ver=2018-10-17-112418-240 .

transitions.title: A held dominant releases the song again
transitions.how: The quieter episode gathers into F-major harmony, held and then rearticulated before the Venus song returns in B♭ major. F now functions as the dominant of that destination, giving the broad restatement a clear harmonic launch. At Tempo I the full band restores the stronger pulse and weight, while flowing accompaniment continues below the tune. This is the central song, not the pilgrims’ hymn: Wagner raises its tonal level and rebuilds its surroundings before the overture’s final change of allegiance.
transitions.evidence: Renewed fast span is mapped at 550 s. F-centred sustained sound at 8:50–9:05 precedes the rise and B♭-major estimates from 9:15. Sousa’s score, printed pp. 49–50, shows the dominant preparation and Tempo I at rehearsal E. The relations file matches the Venus song at 566–600.5 s with its earlier statement, five semitones higher: https://www.marineband.marines.mil/Portals/175/Docs/Sheet%20Music/Tannhauser/tannhauser_score.pdf?ver=2018-10-17-112418-240 .

transitions.title: The hymn returns above surviving motion
transitions.how: The fast music loses its massed attacks and recedes towards the B♭-major home region. The pilgrims’ long phrases can then return in the middle and lower wind voices, but the fast surface is not simply switched off: the first clarinets keep their running line around the chorale. The bass supplies a steadier harmonic footing while sustained notes become the foreground. The seam changes which layer commands attention, allowing the two kinds of motion to coexist before the closing hymn reaches full strength.
transitions.evidence: The pilgrims return is mapped at 665 s, during the sharp level retreat at 11:05–11:10. Sousa’s score, printed pp. 62–66, preserves running clarinets under the returning chorale. The relations file matches the hymn at 674–688 s with its first broad statement. This is not labelled a literal restoration of the opening tempo or metre: https://www.marineband.marines.mil/Portals/175/Docs/Sheet%20Music/Tannhauser/tannhauser_score.pdf?ver=2018-10-17-112418-240 .

transitions.title: The returning hymn takes the whole band
transitions.how: The returning chorale grows out of its quieter statement rather than being replaced at the final expansion. Sousa adds the upper winds and weight of the full brass to the sustained line, while the first clarinets continue their rapid figuration and the low instruments keep the bass moving. B♭ major remains the home key. The registral spread and stronger doublings make the hymn dominate the very motion that had threatened to displace it: the conclusion combines the two textures instead of silencing one.
transitions.evidence: Final hymn and close is mapped at 760 s, in the measured expansion at 12:35–12:45. Sousa’s score, printed pp. 76–79, shows the accumulating doublings and full-band hymn at rehearsal H with continuing clarinet figuration. Its precise entrance is not assigned to 760 s: https://www.marineband.marines.mil/Portals/175/Docs/Sheet%20Music/Tannhauser/tannhauser_score.pdf?ver=2018-10-17-112418-240 .

facts: Composition with Theodor Weinlig in Leipzig; practical theatre work in Würzburg, Magdeburg, Königsberg and Riga
Royal Saxon Kapellmeister, Dresden, 1843–49; founder of the Bayreuth Festival, first held in 1876
Wrote his own librettos, alongside extensive and often polemical prose
Thirteen completed operas; the four-part Ring; songs, orchestral works and piano music
composer.background:
Wagner grew up among actors, singers and theatrical households in Leipzig and Dresden. His father died in 1813; his mother subsequently married the actor and painter Ludwig Geyer. Literature preceded serious musical training: as a schoolboy Wagner attempted a tragedy before he had mastered composition. Beethoven’s symphonies and Weber’s operas supplied different models, one for the weight of an orchestral argument, the other for a German theatre of supernatural events and sharply characterised instruments. Lessons with Theodor Weinlig in 1831 gave him a grounding in counterpoint. The later claim to have rebuilt opera came from someone who first learned its routines as a working theatre musician.

He held posts in Würzburg, Magdeburg, Königsberg and Riga, married the actress Minna Planer in 1836, and repeatedly found himself in debt. His early operas tried incompatible languages: Die Feen follows German Romantic opera, while Das Liebesverbot, after Shakespeare’s Measure for Measure, adopts a more Italianate manner. In 1839 the Wagners fled Riga and travelled by sea to London, then to Paris. There he copied, arranged and wrote journalism while trying to enter the operatic establishment. Meyerbeer, whom Wagner would later attack, helped him obtain a hearing for Rienzi. Wagner knew the grand-opera machinery of public ceremony, political catastrophe and large chorus from practical experience.
composer.epithet: An opera composer who made the orchestra remember what the characters conceal, and built a theatre for the result.
